blocks.text: On 1 January 1914, Sir Frederick Lugard signed two protectorates into one Nigeria. The name was new; the method of ruling was not. In Kano an emir still sat in his palace, now answering to a British resident. In an Igbo village a 'warrant chief' who had never been a king was handed a cap of office. That difference — using real chiefs in the North, inventing them in the East — is the story of indirect rule, and the grievance that fed Nigerian nationalism.

blocks.title: Amalgamation and indirect rule
blocks.text: AMALGAMATION (1 January 1914) was Lugard's unification of the Colony and Protectorate of Southern Nigeria with the Protectorate of Northern Nigeria into a single Colony and Protectorate of Nigeria. INDIRECT RULE was the British method of governing through existing traditional authorities, supervised by colonial residents and district officers, rather than replacing those authorities with a wholly British administration.

blocks.markdown:
### Why amalgamation, and how indirect rule worked

Lugard and the Colonial Office wanted **administrative economy**: the cash-crop South could subsidise the cash-poor North, and one railway, one army and one civil service were cheaper than two. Amalgamation did not create a shared political community; the North and South kept separate administrations for years, and Northern leaders were not brought into the Southern Legislative Council until the Richards Constitution of 1946.

Indirect rule, which Lugard had practised in the North, rested on traditional rulers collecting tax, keeping order and running native courts, while British officials issued instructions and reserved the right to depose a non-compliant chief.

It **succeeded most in the North**, where emirates already had emirs, alkali courts and district heads. It worked **less well in the West**, where the Alaafin's power had declined and an educated elite already questioned chiefs. It **failed in the East**, which was largely acephalous: the British created **warrant chiefs** who lacked traditional legitimacy. The **Aba Women's Riot of 1929** was in part a revolt against those warrant chiefs and against taxation.

### Causes and phases of Nigerian nationalism

**Nationalism** here means the movement of Nigerians to end colonial rule and to govern themselves.

**Causes:** Western education and missionary schools, which produced a literate elite able to use the colonial language against the colonial power; racial discrimination in the civil service and social clubs; the experience of the two World Wars, in which Africans fought for 'freedom' they were denied at home; the **Atlantic Charter** (1941) and the independence of India (1947); economic exploitation and taxation; the growth of a nationalist press; and the formation of political associations.

**Phases.** Early or proto-nationalism was cultural and local: newspapers, the Lagos elite, and Herbert Macaulay's **Nigerian National Democratic Party (NNDP, 1923)**, which used the Clifford Constitution's tiny elective principle. Political nationalism broadened in the 1930s and 1940s with the **Nigerian Youth Movement (NYM, 1934)** and the **NCNC (1944)**, then became a struggle for self-government through regional parties — AG, NPC, NCNC — in the 1950s, ending in independence on **1 October 1960**.

items: **1922–1930s** — Clifford elective principle; NNDP dominates Lagos elections; press agitation.
**1934–1944** — NYM offers a broader, more national youth platform; later splits, after which Azikiwe leaves.
**1944–1951** — NCNC founded (Macaulay president, Azikiwe secretary); Richards Constitution protested; Macpherson process begins.

blocks.title: Why indirect rule succeeded in the North and failed in the East
blocks.prompt: Using the pre-colonial systems you already know, explain the uneven success of indirect rule in Nigeria.

steps.text: State the method: Britain governed through existing rulers, supervised by residents, to save money and reduce resistance.

North: emirates already had emirs, hakimai, alkali courts and a habit of taxation. Lugard could issue an order to an emir and it would travel down a familiar hierarchy. Success was structural, not because Northerners 'preferred' colonialism.

West: a monarchy existed, so the method could be tried, but the Alaafin's authority was weaker than in the eighteenth century, and an educated elite in Lagos and Ibadan challenged both chief and resident.
East: most Igbo communities were acephalous. There was no king to 'use'. Warrant chiefs were invented, lacked legitimacy, and became associated with taxation and abuse — hence the 1929 Women's Riot.
Link to nationalism: the same educated elite that indirect rule shut out of real power became the leadership of NNDP, NYM and NCNC.

blocks.answer: Indirect rule fitted the centralised emirate; it fitted Oyo only partly; it failed among acephalous Igbo communities, where warrant chiefs had to be invented. That misfit, plus exclusion of the educated elite, fed nationalist organisation

blocks.title: Dates that must not be swapped
blocks.text: Amalgamation 1914; Clifford Constitution and first elective principle 1922; NNDP 1923; NYM 1934; NCNC 1944; independence 1 October 1960. Lugard is amalgamation and indirect rule, not independence. Macaulay is early nationalism, not the first Prime Minister — that was Tafawa Balewa. Azikiwe became President in 1963, not Prime Minister.

points: The 1914 amalgamation united the Northern and Southern protectorates under Lugard, mainly for administrative economy; it did not create political unity.
Indirect rule governed through traditional authorities. It worked best in the North, less well in the West, and failed in the East, where warrant chiefs were imposed.
Nigerian nationalism was caused by Western education, discrimination, the World Wars, the Atlantic Charter, economic grievances, the press and political associations.
Phases run from early NNDP politics (1923) through NYM (1934) and NCNC (1944) to the regional parties and independence in 1960.
Key leaders: Herbert Macaulay, Nnamdi Azikiwe, Obafemi Awolowo, Ahmadu Bello and Abubakar Tafawa Balewa.
